scene: Inferno XXVI — Ulysses and Diomedes together in one divided flame; Ulysses recounts his final voyage
story: Dante and Virgil reach the eighth bolgia, where fraudulent counselors are enclosed within moving flames; Dante compares their multitude to fireflies seen from a hillside.
A flame with two horns or tongues approaches. Virgil identifies its two occupants as Ulysses and Diomedes, associated with shared stratagems in the Trojan War.
Dante wishes to hear them; Virgil addresses the flame and asks for an account. The greater tip moves as Ulysses begins speaking; Diomedes does not separately speak in this canto.

Ulysses recounts how he left the familiar world behind, persuaded his aging companions to seek knowledge and experience beyond the Pillars of Hercules, and sailed for five months into the southern ocean.
They glimpse a vast mountain in the distance, rejoice briefly, and a whirlwind strikes their vessel, spinning it and sinking it.
The flame falls silent and departs. The shared enclosure has not made the two named occupants identical, nor their voices interchangeable.
